title: How aluminium is made and why it matters
summary: Before aluminium becomes the shiny metal we all recognise, it starts as bauxite, a reddish-brown ore found in the ground. Bauxite is mined and processed into a fine white powder called alumina which is then used to produce aluminium.
body_markdown:
We also have support from the Queensland and Australian governments to help secure internationally competitive energy to continue aluminium production at Boyne smelter until at least 2040.


Together, these agreements help preserve Queensland’s fully integrated aluminium value chain from bauxite mining to smelting and supports thousands of regional jobs and onshore manufacturing.


They also position Boyne smelter to be one of the world’s first aluminium smelters underpinned by solar and wind power, making Rio Tinto Australia’s largest industrial offtaker of renewable energy.


In New South Wales,[Tomago Aluminium](https://www.riotinto.com/en/operations/anz/tomago) has also secured a[long-term pathway](https://www.riotinto.com/en/news/releases/2026/rio-tinto-welcomes-agreement-to-secure-long-term-future-of-tomago-aluminium) for its energy supply. A new 10-year power purchase agreement will provide electricity to the smelter through to 2038, with 100% renewable electricity from 2033, supporting the long-term future of Australia’s largest aluminium smelter.


### 2. Research and innovation


#### What technologies are changing aluminium smelting?


Technology is changing how we produce aluminium: providing the potential for more metal, more efficiently with fewer emissions.


One example is **[AP60](https://www.riotinto.com/en/news/releases/2026/rio-tinto-commissions-1-5-billion-ap60-smelter-expansion-in-quebec)** , is our proprietary aluminium smelting technology.


It’s designed to produce more aluminium per cell than conventional smelting technologies, helping improve productivity and efficiency.
